claims.text: The initial particles are sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
The initial nanoparticles form a disordered solid solution.
The sluggish-diffusion regime breaks down above 600 K.
Surface-energy-driven segregation causes the breakdown of sluggish diffusion.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than Co, Ni, and Pt in this nanoparticle system.
Au and Cu diffuse rapidly toward the nanoparticle surface or coalesce during heating.
Co, Ni, and Pt segregate to the core or form distinct phases during heating.
The constituent elements have sufficiently different diffusion coefficients to drive segregation.
Bulk lattice diffusion can have high activation energies in related high-entropy alloys.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-10 nm particles allows surface diffusion to dominate over bulk lattice diffusion.
Ostwald ripening causes preferential loss of the smallest particles.
Surface curvature and chemical-potential gradients drive the proposed Ostwald ripening.
Surface-energy minimization changes the particles from spherical to faceted, elongated, or irregular shapes.
Heating produces a significant decrease in particle number density, concentrated among the smallest particles.
Heating produces a non-uniform elemental distribution with Au and Cu enriched at the surface.
The remaining particles deviate from equiatomic bulk composition after heating.
Under the sluggish-diffusion baseline, a single-phase solid solution would show minimal structural evolution up to 1000 K.
For bulk samples or particles larger than 50 nm, sluggish diffusion may preserve the single-phase structure.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis specifies breakdown above 600 K, while the uncertainty field states that the exact crossover temperature is unknown without direct measurement.
